6added-- # Hoare: Hoare Logic, Part I
7added

48added-- HIDE: This file and all later ones should make a habit
49added-- of always presenting both syntax and semantics of new
50added-- language constructs in informal style as well as formal.
51added-- See MoreStlc.v for a template.
52added
53added-- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work
54added-- through some simple examples of *program verification* --
55added-- i.e., to use the precise definition of Imp to prove formally
56added-- that particular programs satisfy particular specifications
57added-- of their behavior.
58added
59added-- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic*
60added-- -- often shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of
61added-- the syntactic constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic
62added-- "proof rule" that can be used to reason compositionally
63added-- about the correctness of programs involving this construct.
64added
65added-- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of
66added-- writing down *specifications* of programs, and a *structured
67added-- proof technique* for proving that programs are correct with
68added-- respect to such specifications -- where by "structured" we
69added-- mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors the
70added-- structure of the programs that they are about.
71added
72added-- Note to developers:
73added-- `HIDE: MRC'20: The terse version used to start with just an outline of
74added-- what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
75added-- The text above seems like a better intro.
76added--
77added-- MRC'20: this is the former terse intro.
78added--
79added-- What we've done so far:
80added--
81added-- - Formalized Imp
82added-- - identifiers and states
83added-- - abstract syntax trees
84added-- - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
85added-- - evaluation relation (for commands)
86added--
87added-- - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
88added-- - determinism of evaluation
89added-- - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
90added-- definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
91added-- arithmetic expression evaluation)
92added-- - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
93added-- - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
94added-- - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
95added--
96added-- We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
97added-- - Termination
98added-- - Nontermination
99added-- - Equivalence
100added--
101added-- Topic:
102added-- - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
103added-- correctness_ of programs in Imp
104added--
105added-- Goals:
106added-- - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
107added-- - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
108added--
109added-- Plan:
110added-- - specifications (assertions / Hoare triples)
111added-- - proof rules
112added-- - loop invariants
113added-- - decorated programs
114added-- - examples`
115added
116added-- ## Assertions
117added
118addedopen scoped MyGetElem
119added
120added-- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a
121added-- program's memory -- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
122added
123addedabbrev Assertion := State → Prop
124added
125added-- Note to developers:
126added-- HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the
127added-- quiz/optional exercise so that there would be some
128added-- modeling of the kinds of answers we expect.
129added
130added-- For example,
131added
132added-- - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value
133added-- of `X` is `3`,
134added
135added-- - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
136added
137added-- - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
138added
139added-- _Quiz:_
140added
141added-- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e., say
142added-- which states satisfy them)
143added
144added-- (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
145added
146added-- (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
147added
148added-- (C)
149added-- `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`

261addedopen Lean Elab Term

263addedscoped syntax:max (name := assn) "assn(" ident "; " term ")" : term
264addedscoped syntax "{{" term "}}" : term
265added
266added@[term_elab assn]
267addeddef assnElab : TermElab := fun stx type? => do
268added match stx with
269added | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
270added let t ← elabTerm t none
271added let ty ← Meta.inferType t
272added dbg_trace ty
273added -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
274added if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
275added return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
276added (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
277added (mkConst ``String)
278added (mkConst ``Nat)
279added (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
280added (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
281added (mkConst ``String)
282added (mkConst ``Nat))
283added (← elabTerm st none) t
284added if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
285added return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
286added else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
287added return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
288added else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
289added return t
290added else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
291added return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
292added else
293added return t
294added | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
295added
296added-- `: Assertion` guards that the resulting type is `State → Prop`.
297addedmacro_rules
298added | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))
299added
300addedmacro_rules
301added | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))
302added | `(assn($st; $l = $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) = assn($st; $r))
303added | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
304added | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
305added | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
306added | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
307added | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
308added | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
309added | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
310added | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
311added | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
312added | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
313added | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
314added | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
315added | `(assn($st; $f $a1)) => ``($f assn($st; $a1))
316added | `(assn($st; $f $a1 $a2)) => ``($f assn($st; $a1) assn($st; $a2))
317added -- | `(assn($st; $f $t*)) => ``($f ) -- TODO how to get arbitrary applications
318addedend

341added-- TODO OUTDATED We will sometimes need to lift functions to
342added-- operate on assertion expressions:
343added
344added-- `{{ #f e1 .. en }}` stands for
345added-- `(fun st => f (e1 st) .. (en st))`
346added
347added-- Note to developers:
348added-- NOTATION: This notation should come early so that later
349added-- notations for arithmetic expressions take precedence for
350added-- printing. Otherwise `{{ X + X }}` would print as
351added-- `{{ #add X Y }}`.
352added
353added-- We can "escape" a raw Lean function using a `~` prefix:
354added
355added-- For example: `{{ ~(fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0) }}`
356added
357added-- Note to developers:
358added-- NOTATION: SAZ 2024: It is important that this custom
359added-- notation be at a level higher than 1 when added to the
360added-- `constr` grammar because it interacts with the
361added-- "application" case of `com` and the notation for Hoare
362added-- triples. That grammar parses embedded function arguments
363added-- at level 1. We never want `f {{P}}` to parse `{ P }` as
364added-- an assertion when used in a command. Instead we want
365added-- `{{P}}` to "close" the Hoare triple.
366added--
367added-- `NOTATION: Note for Rocq custom grammar hackers. From what I can tell, the
368added-- Rocq LL(1) parser does left-factorize the grammar, *however* it uses a very
369added-- strict notion of what counts as "equal" for the purposes of the factorization.
370added-- In particular, a grammar entry might have a level,
371added-- as in [e custom assn at level 99] in the notation below. Leaving out the
372added-- "at level 99" is *semantically equivalent*, because the [assn] grammar starts
373added-- at that level, but omitting it will not work because the grammar for
374added-- Hoare triples below includes "at level 99" -- the [LEVEL "99"] part of the
375added-- grammar counts for factorization.
376added--
377added-- The upshot is that means that this notation and the Hoare triple notation
378added-- (which overlaps with [{{ _ }}]) must be changed in tandem and use identical
379added-- level specifications.`

406added-- ### Assertion Implication
407added
408added-- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies*
409added-- `Q`, written `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state
410added-- `st`, `Q` also holds.
411added
412addeddef AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
413added ∀ st, P st → Q st
414added
415added-- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is
416added-- analogous to the "usual" Lean implication `→`.
417added
418addednotation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
419added
420addedtheorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
421added
422added-- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between
423added-- assertions:
424added
425addednotation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
426added
427added-- Note to developers (Claude):
428added-- The Rocq source puts these notations in a
429added-- `hoare_spec_scope`, with a book comment explaining that
430added-- "the `hoare_spec_scope` annotation tells Rocq that this
431added-- notation is not global but is intended to be used in
432added-- particular contexts." Lean has no notation scopes, so
433added-- the notations are simply global and that paragraph is
434added-- omitted.
435added
436added-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
437added
438added-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after
439added-- executing a command:
440added
441added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
442added
443added-- This means:
444added
445added-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying
446added-- assertion `P`,
447added
448added-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
449added
450added-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
451added
452added-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple,
453added-- and `Q` is the *postcondition*.
454added
455added-- For example,
456added
457added-- - The Hoare triple
458added
459added-- {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
460added
461added-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in
462added-- which `X = 0` to a state in which `X = 1`.
463added
464added-- - On the other hand,
465added
466added-- ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
467added
468added-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
469added-- `{{X = m}} X :=
470added-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice
471added-- of `m`. Note that `m` in the two assertions is a reference
472added-- to the *Lean* variable `m`, which is bound outside the Hoare
473added-- triple.
474added
475added-- _Quiz:_
476added
477added-- Paraphrase the following in English.
478added
479added-- 1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
480added
481added-- 2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
482added
483added-- 3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
484added
485added-- 4) {{True}} c {{False}}
486added
487added-- 5) ∀ m,
488added-- {{X = m}}
489added-- c
490added-- {{Y = real_fact m}}
491added
492added-- 6) ∀ m,
493added-- {{X = m}}
494added-- c
495added-- {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
496added

500added-- claimed relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
501added
502added-- {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}

504added-- (A) Yes

592added-- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
593added
594added-- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
595added
596addeddef ValidHoareTriple
597added (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
598added ∀ st st',
599added (st =[ c ]=> st') →
600added P st →
601added Q st'
602added
603added-- Note to developers:
604added-- `NOTATION: SAZ 2024 One trickiness of these notations is that we
605added-- want the [com] and [assn] grammars to be "open", so that they can
606added-- include expressions parsed by the full [constr] grammar of Rocq.
607added-- However, then there is a conflict of precedence of the
608added-- "application" cases:
609added--
610added-- The example " {{ True }} X := 0 {{ False }} " does not parse as
611added-- intended because the [com] grammar includes the capability of
612added-- parsing the (ill-typed) term "0 {{ False }}".
613added--
614added-- This means that the "application" for [com] should disallow
615added-- arguments at the level at which the [assn] grammar is included
616added-- in constr. The upshot is that this notation should be included
617added-- in the grammar at the *same* level as the assertion notation
618added-- [{{ P }}], which is 2.`
619added
620added-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two
621added-- assertions is parsed with the same grammar as the
622added-- `imp { … }` notation, so a command that is a Lean variable
623added-- (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`, just
624added-- as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
625added
626addedopen scoped Assertion
627added
628addednamespace ValidHoareTriple
629added
630added/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
631addedscoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
632added
633addedmacro_rules
634added | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
635added `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
636added
637addedend ValidHoareTriple
638added
639addedsection
640addedopen scoped ValidHoareTriple

665added-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_post_true ⭐
666added
667added-- Prove that if `Q` holds in every state, then any triple with
668added-- `Q` as its postcondition is valid.
669added
670addedtheorem hoare_post_true (P Q : Assertion) (c : Com) (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
671added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
672added sorry
673added
674added-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false ⭐
675added
676added-- Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with
677added-- `P` as its precondition is valid.
678added
679addedtheorem hoare_pre_false (P Q : Assertion) (c : Com) (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
680added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
681added sorry
682added
683added-- ## Proof Rules
684added
685added-- We want to be able to *prove* Hoare triples formally.
686added
687added-- Here's our plan:
688added
689added-- - introduce one "proof rule" for each Imp syntactic form
690added
691added-- - plus a couple of "structural rules" that help glue proofs
692added-- together
693added
694added-- - prove these rules correct in terms of the definition of
695added-- `ValidHoareTriple`
696added
697added-- - prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever
698added-- unfolding the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`
699added
700added-- ### Skip
701added
702added-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any
703added-- assertion `P`:
704added
705added-- -------------------- (hoare_skip)
706added-- {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
707added
708addedtheorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
709added {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
710added intro st st' h hp
711added inversion h
712added assumption
713added
714added-- ### Sequencing
715added
716added-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state
717added-- where `Q` holds, and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds
718added-- to one where `R` holds, then doing `c1` followed by `c2`
719added-- will take any state where `P` holds to one where `R` holds:
720added
721added-- {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
722added-- {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
723added-- ---------------------- (hoare_seq)
724added-- {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
725added
726addedtheorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
727added (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
728added {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{ R }} := by
729added intro st st' h12 pre
730added inversion h12 with
731added | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
732added exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
733added
734added-- ### Assignment
735added
736added-- How can we complete this triple?
737added
738added-- {{ ??? }} X := Y {{ X = 1 }}
739added
740added-- One natural possibility is:
741added
742added-- {{ Y = 1 }} X := Y {{ X = 1 }}
743added
744added-- The precondition is just the postcondition, but with `X`
745added-- replaced by `Y`.
746added
747added-- How about this one?
748added
749added-- {{ ??? }} X := X + Y {{ X = 1 }}
750added
751added-- Replace `X` with `X + Y`:
752added
753added-- {{ X + Y = 1 }} X := X + Y {{ X = 1 }}
754added
755added-- This works because "equals 1" holding of `X` is guaranteed
756added-- by the property "equals 1" holding of whatever is being
757added-- assigned to `X`.
758added
759added-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary
760added-- assertion `Q`, and the right-hand side of the assignment
761added-- could be some arbitrary arithmetic expression `a`:
762added
763added-- {{ ??? }} X := a {{ Q }}
764added
765added-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences
766added-- of `X` in it replaced by `a`.
767added
768added-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing
769added-- occurrences: Define `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is
770added-- substituted in place of `X`".
771added
772added-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
773added
774added-- {{ Q [X ↦ a] }} X := a {{ Q }}
775added
776added-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement
777added-- `X := a` to terminate in a state that satisfies assertion
778added-- `Q`, then it suffices to start in a state that also
779added-- satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted for every
780added-- occurrence of `X`.
781added
782added-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
783added
784added-- {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }} (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
785added-- X := X + 1
786added-- {{ X ≤ 5 }}
787added
788added-- {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }} (that is, 3 = 3)
789added-- X := 3
790added-- {{ X = 3 }}
791added
792added-- {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}. (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
793added-- X := 3
794added-- {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
795added
796added-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of
797added-- "substituting an expression for an Imp variable in an
798added-- assertion", which we refer to as assertion substitution, or
799added-- `Assertion.sub`.
800added
801added-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an
802added-- arithmetic expression `a`, we want to derive another
803added-- proposition `P'` that is just the same as `P` except that
804added-- `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
805added
806added-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp
807added-- expressions for Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv*
808added-- (`subst_aexp` and friends). The difference is that, here,
809added-- `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't directly
810added-- "edit" its text.
811added
812added-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in
813added-- an updated state, defined as follows:
814added
815addeddef Assertion.sub (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
816added fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
817added
818added-- Note to developers (before next release):
819added-- This concrete syntax is hard to read in comments because
820added-- of all the square brackets. Something like
821added-- `P with X ↦ a` would be much better. I guess the same
822added-- will apply to the lambda-calculus chapters... BCP 25: I
823added-- still think this is a good idea, and I had a quick go at
824added-- implementing it, but did not succeed yet.
825added
826added-- TODO Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)
827added
828added/-- Assertion substitution: `P [X ↦ a]` -/
829addedsyntax:100 term:100 " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
830added
831addedmacro_rules
832added | `($P [$x ↦ $a]) => `(Assertion.sub $x (aexp { $a }) $P)
833added -- | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a])) => ``(assn($st; $P) [$x ↦ $a]) -- maybe we could push substitutions inside
834added
835added-- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
836added
837added-- P [ X ↦ a ]
838added
839added#check (fun st => Assertion.sub X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
840added#check {{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]
841added#check (∀ st, ({{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]) st)
842added
843added-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call
844added-- it `P'` -- that behaves just like `P` except that, wherever
845added-- `P` looks up the variable `X` in the current state, `P'`
846added-- instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
847added
848added-- We can demonstrate formally that we have captured intuitive
849added-- meaning of "assertion subsitution" by proving some example
850added-- logical equivalences:
851added
852addednamespace ExampleAssertionSub
853addedexample :
854added {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ 3] <<->> {{ 3 ≤ 5 }} := by
855added constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
856added
857addedexample :
858added {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ X + 1] <<->> {{ (X + 1) ≤ 5 }} := by
859added constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
860added
861addedend ExampleAssertionSub

1081added
1082added-- Now, using the substitution operation we've just defined, we
1083added-- can give the precise proof rule for assignment:
1084added
1085added-- ---------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1086added-- {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X := a {{Q}}
1087added
1088added-- We can prove formally that this rule is indeed valid.
1089added
1090addedtheorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
1091added {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }} x := ~a; {{ Q }} := by
1092added intro st st' hE hQ
1093added inversion hE with
1094added | asgn n h =>
1095added subst h
1096added exact hQ
1097added
1098added-- Here's a first formal proof of a Hoare triple using this
1099added-- rule.
1100added
1101addedtheorem assertion_sub_example :
1102added {{ {{ X < 5 }} [X ↦ X + 1] }}
1103added X := X + 1;
1104added {{ X < 5 }} := by
1105added apply hoare_asgn
1106added
1107added-- Of course, we'd probably prefer to work with this simpler
1108added-- triple:
1109added
1110added-- {{X < 4}} X := X + 1 {{X < 5}}
1111added
1112added-- We will see how to do so in the next section.
1113added
1114added-- Several proofs below use the facts about total-map updates
1115added-- proved in the *Typeclasses* chapter -- `TotalMap.update_eq`,
1116added-- `TotalMap.update_neq`, `TotalMap.update_shadow`,
1117added-- `TotalMap.update_same`, and `TotalMap.update_permute`. Make
1118added-- sure you understand their statements.
1119added
1120added-- ### Consequence
1121added
1122added-- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from
1123added-- the Hoare rules won't quite be the ones we want in the
1124added-- particular situation at hand -- they may be logically
1125added-- equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails to
1126added-- unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually
1127added-- may be logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for
1128added-- postconditions) than what we need.
1129added
1130added-- For instance,
1131added
1132added-- {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1133added
1134added-- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1135added
1136added-- {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1137added
1138added-- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of
1139added-- `hoare_asgn` because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not
1140added-- syntactically equal assertions.
1141added
1142added-- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple
1143added-- is valid, then the other must certainly be as well. We can
1144added-- capture this observation with the following rule:
1145added
1146added-- {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1147added-- P <<->> P'
1148added-- ---------------------
1149added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1150added
1151added-- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that
1152added-- strengthening the precondition or weakening the
1153added-- postcondition of a valid triple always produces another
1154added-- valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules of
1155added-- Consequence*.
1156added
1157added-- {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1158added-- P ->> P'
1159added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence_pre)
1160added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1161added
1162added-- {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1163added-- Q' ->> Q
1164added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence_post)
1165added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1166added
1167added-- Here are the formal versions:
1168added
1169addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1170added (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1171added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1172added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1173added intro st st' heval hpre
1174added apply hhoare st st'
1175added · assumption
1176added · apply himp
1177added assumption
1178added
1179addedtheorem hoare_consequence_post (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1180added (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1181added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1182added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1183added intro st st' heval hpre
1184added apply himp
1185added apply hhoare st st'
1186added · assumption
1187added · assumption
1188added
1189added-- For example, we can use the first consequence rule like
1190added-- this:
1191added
1192added-- {{ True }} ->>
1193added-- {{ (X = 1) [X ↦ 1] }}
1194added-- X := 1
1195added-- {{ X = 1 }}
1196added
1197added-- Or, formally...
1198added
1199addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1 :
1200added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1201added sorry
1202added
1203added-- We can also use it to prove the example mentioned earlier.
1204added
1205added-- {{ X < 4 }} ->>
1206added-- {{ (X < 5)[X ↦ X + 1] }}
1207added-- X := X + 1
1208added-- {{ X < 5 }}
1209added
1210added-- Or, formally ...
1211added
1212addedtheorem assertion_sub_example2 :
1213added {{X < 4}}
1214added X := X + 1;
1215added {{X < 5}} := by
1216added sorry
1217added
1218added-- Finally, here is a combined rule of consequence that allows
1219added-- us to vary both the precondition and the postcondition.
1220added
1221added-- {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1222added-- P ->> P'
1223added-- Q' ->> Q
1224added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence)
1225added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1226added
1227addedtheorem hoare_consequence (P P' Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1228added (htriple : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :
1229added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1230added apply hoare_consequence_pre (P' := P')
1231added · apply hoare_consequence_post (Q' := Q')
1232added · assumption
1233added · assumption
1234added · assumption
1235added
1236added-- ### Automation
1237added
1238added-- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples
1239added-- can be streamlined using the automation techniques that we
1240added-- introduced in the *Automation* chapter of *Logical
1241added-- Foundations*.
1242added
1243added-- Recall that the `simp` tactic can be told to unfold
1244added-- definitions as part of its simplifications. The definitions
1245added-- we keep needing to unfold in this chapter are
1246added-- `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, `Assertion.sub`, the
1247added-- lifting functions `Assertion.ofProp`, `Aexp'.ofNat`, and
1248added-- `Aexp'.ofAexp`, and the total-map operations. We'll pass
1249added-- these to `simp` explicitly below (and shortly package the
1250added-- recipe up as a tactic of our own).
1251added
1252added-- Note to developers (Claude):
1253added-- The Rocq source here registers
1254added-- `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1255added-- t_update : core`
1256added-- for `auto`. That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the
1257added-- `Arguments /.` commands, it does not affect `simpl`), so
1258added-- its Lean counterpart is the `assertion_auto` tactic's
1259added-- simp list below -- not global `@[simp]` lemmas as for
1260added-- the notation wrappers, whose folded names carry no
1261added-- meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.sub` do.
1262added
1263added-- Here's a good candidate for automation:
1264added
1265addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1266added (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1267added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1268added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1269added intro st st' heval hpre
1270added apply hhoare st st'
1271added · assumption
1272added · apply himp
1273added assumption
1274added
1275added-- `apply` will find `st` for us, using a metavariable.
1276added
1277addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1278added (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1279added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1280added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1281added intro st st' heval hpre
1282added apply hhoare
1283added · assumption
1284added · apply himp
1285added assumption
1286added
1287added-- Since the remaining steps just apply hypotheses to each
1288added-- other, the entire proof can actually be compressed into a
1289added-- single line, by writing the term that `exact`ly proves the
1290added-- conclusion.
1291added
1292addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre'''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1293added (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1294added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1295added intro st st' heval hpre
1296added exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
1297added
1298added-- ...as can the proof for the postcondition consequence rule.
1299added
1300addedtheorem hoare_consequence_post' (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1301added (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1302added {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1303added intro st st' heval hpre
1304added exact himp st' (hhoare st st' heval hpre)
1305added
1306added-- We can also use a metavariable to streamline a proof
1307added-- (`hoare_asgn_example1`), that we did earlier as an example
1308added-- of using the consequence rule:
1309added
1310addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1' :
1311added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1312added apply hoare_consequence_pre -- no need to state an assertion
1313added · apply hoare_asgn
1314added · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1315added intro st _
1316added rfl
1317added
1318added-- The final bullet of that proof also looks like a candidate
1319added-- for automation.
1320added
1321addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1'' :
1322added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1323added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1324added · apply hoare_asgn
1325added · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, TotalMap.update_eq]
1326added
1327added-- Now we have quite a nice proof script: it simply identifies
1328added-- the Hoare rules that need to be used and leaves the
1329added-- remaining low-level details up to Lean to figure out.
1330added
1331added-- The other example of using consequence that we did earlier,
1332added-- `hoare_asgn_example2`, requires a little more work to
1333added-- automate. `simp` simplifies the assertion implication in the
1334added-- final bullet, but cannot finish it: the leftover goal is
1335added-- arithmetic, so it needs `lia`.
1336added
1337addedtheorem assertion_sub_example2' :
1338added {{X < 4}}
1339added X := X + 1;
1340added {{X < 5}} := by
1341added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1342added · apply hoare_asgn
1343added · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, TotalMap.update_eq] -- an arithmetic goal remains
1344added lia
1345added
1346added-- Let's introduce our own tactic to handle both that bullet
1347added-- and the bullet from example 1. A `macro` declaration gives a
1348added-- name to a canned sequence of tactics:
1349added
1350added/-- Prove routine facts about assertions: unfold the Hoare-logic
1351addeddefinitions and lifting functions, simplify, and finish any leftover
1352addedarithmetic with `lia`. -/
1353addedmacro "assertion_auto" : tactic =>
1354added `(tactic| (intros
1355added <;> try (simp [assertImplies_def, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
1356added TotalMap.update, TotalMap.getElem_def,
1357added W, X, Y, Z] at *)
1358added <;> try lia))
1359added
1360addedtheorem assertion_sub_example2'' :
1361added {{X < 4}}
1362added X := X + 1;
1363added {{X < 5}} := by
1364added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1365added · apply hoare_asgn
1366added · assertion_auto
1367added
1368addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1''' :
1369added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1370added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1371added · apply hoare_asgn
1372added · assertion_auto
1373added
1374added-- Again, we have quite a nice proof script. All the low-level
1375added-- details of proofs about assertions have been taken care of
1376added-- automatically. Of course, `assertion_auto` isn't able to
1377added-- prove everything we could possibly want to know about
1378added-- assertions -- there's no magic here! But it's pretty good.
1379added
1380added-- ### Sequencing + Assignment
1381added
1382added-- Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and
1383added-- assignment. Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with
1384added-- `hoare_consequence_pre` and `apply`'s metavariables.
1385added
1386addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1387added {{a = n}}
1388added X := ~a;
1389added skip;
1390added {{X = n}} := by
1391added apply hoare_seq
1392added · -- right part of seq
1393added apply hoare_skip
1394added · -- left part of seq
1395added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1396added · apply hoare_asgn
1397added · assertion_auto
1398added
1399added-- Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the
1400added-- sequencing rule is as a "decorated program" where the
1401added-- intermediate assertion `Q` is written between `c1` and `c2`:
1402added
1403added-- {{ a = n }}
1404added-- X := a
1405added-- {{ X = n }}; <--- decoration for Q
1406added-- skip
1407added-- {{ X = n }}
1408added
1409added-- We'll come back to the idea of decorated programs in much
1410added-- more detail in the next chapter.
1411added
1412added-- ### Conditionals
1413added
1414added-- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional
1415added-- commands?
1416added
1417added-- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing
1418added-- either of the branches, then it holds after the whole
1419added-- conditional. So we might be tempted to write:
1420added
1421added-- {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1422added-- {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1423added-- ---------------------------------
1424added-- {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1425added
1426added-- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule,
1427added-- we cannot show
1428added
1429added-- {{ True }}
1430added-- if X = 0
1431added-- then Y := 2
1432added-- else Y := X + 1
1433added-- end
1434added-- {{ X ≤ Y }}
1435added
1436added-- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in
1437added-- which the assignments take place in the "then" and "else"
1438added-- branches.
1439added
1440added-- Better:
1441added
1442added-- {{P ∧ b}} c1 {{Q}}
1443added-- {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1444added-- ------------------------------------ (hoare_if)
1445added-- {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1446added
1447added-- To make this formal, we need a way of formally "lifting" any
1448added-- bexp `b` to an assertion.
1449added
1450added-- We'll write `bassertion b` for the assertion "the boolean
1451added-- expression `b` evaluates to `true`."
1452added
1453addeddef bassertion (b : Bexp) : Assertion := {{ b }} -- NOTE xhalo32: we don't need this IMO
1454added
1455added@[simp] theorem bassertion_apply (b : Bexp) (st : State) :
1456added bassertion b st = (b.eval st = true) := rfl
1457added
1458addedinstance : Coe Bexp Assertion := ⟨bassertion⟩
1459added
1460added-- A useful fact about `bassertion`:
1461added
1462added-- Note to developers (before next release):
1463added-- `Robert Rand: This isn't an identity but that's because
1464added-- we're using [~(bassertion b st)] in our triples, instead of a more
1465added-- direct/intuitive predicate.
1466added--
1467added-- Some alternatives: 1) P_True b and P_False b (defined directly as
1468added-- desired) 1) bassertion b false (adds relevant argument to bassertion)
1469added-- 2) ((bassertion (!b)) st) (clearer, but less direct).`
1470added
1471addedtheorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
1472added ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1473added simp [h]
1474added
1475added-- Note to developers (One An @meluge):
1476added-- The Rocq proof is the single tactic `congruence`. Using
1477added-- simp seems to work but should we build our own
1478added-- `congruence` tactic?
1479added
1480added-- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals
1481added-- and prove it correct.
1482added
1483added-- The statement of the rule reads: given
1484added-- `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1485added-- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1486added-- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1487added
1488added-- That is (unwrapping the notations):
1489added
1490added-- theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
1491added-- (htrue : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ bassertion b st) c1 Q)
1492added-- (hfalse : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ ¬ (bassertion b st)) c2 Q) :
1493added-- ValidHoareTriple P (Com.cond b c1 c2) Q
1494added
1495addedtheorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
1496added (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1497added {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1498added intro st st' hE hP
1499added inversion hE with
1500added | ifTrue hb hc => exact htrue _ _ hc ⟨hP, hb⟩
1501added | ifFalse hb hc => exact hfalse _ _ hc ⟨hP, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
1502added
1503added-- #### Example
1504added
1505addedtheorem if_example :
1506added {{True}}
1507added if (X = 0) {
1508added Y := 2;
1509added } else {
1510added Y := X + 1;
1511added }
1512added {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1513added apply hoare_if
1514added · -- Then
1515added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1516added · apply hoare_asgn
1517added · -- `assertion_auto` makes no progress here
1518added unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1519added intro st ⟨_, h⟩
1520added simp only [Bexp.eval_eq, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num, beq_iff_eq] at h
1521added rw [TotalMap.update_neq (by decide), TotalMap.update_eq, h]
1522added simp
1523added · -- Else
1524added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1525added · apply hoare_asgn
1526added · assertion_auto
1527added
1528added-- As we did earlier, it would be nice to eliminate all the
1529added-- low-level proof script that isn't about the Hoare rules.
1530added-- Unfortunately, the `assertion_auto` tactic we wrote wasn't
1531added-- quite up to the job. Looking at the proof of `if_example`,
1532added-- we can see why: we had to unfold a definition (`bassertion`)
1533added-- that we didn't need in earlier proofs. (The step from the
1534added-- boolean equality test `st[X] == 0` to the equation
1535added-- `st[X] = 0` is handled by lemmas `simp` already knows, such
1536added-- as `beq_iff_eq`.) So, let's add the unfolding into our
1537added-- tactic.
1538added
1539added-- Note to developers:
1540added-- HIDE: MRC'20: There's probably a better way to engineer
1541added-- this. I don't know Ltac very well though.
1542added
1543added/-- Like `assertion_auto`, but also unfolds `bassertion`, so that facts
1544addedabout the boolean guards of conditionals and loops become available. -/
1545addedmacro "assertion_auto'" : tactic =>
1546added `(tactic| (intros
1547added <;> try (simp [assertImplies_def, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
1548added TotalMap.update, TotalMap.getElem_def,
1549added W, X, Y, Z] at *)
1550added <;> try lia))
1551added
1552added-- Now the proof is quite streamlined.
1553added
1554addedtheorem if_example'' :
1555added {{True}}
1556added if (X = 0) {
1557added Y := 2;
1558added } else {
1559added Y := X + 1;
1560added }
1561added {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1562added apply hoare_if
1563added · apply hoare_consequence_pre
1564added · apply hoare_asgn
1565added · assertion_auto'
1566added · apply hoare_consequence_pre
1567added · apply hoare_asgn
1568added · assertion_auto'
1569added
1570added-- We can even shorten it a little bit more.
1571added
1572addedtheorem if_example''' :
1573added {{True}}
1574added if (X = 0) {
1575added Y := 2;
1576added } else {
1577added Y := X + 1;
1578added }
1579added {{X ≤ Y}} := by
1580added apply hoare_if <;> apply hoare_consequence_pre <;>
1581added (try apply hoare_asgn) <;> try assertion_auto'
1582added
1583added-- Note to developers (Claude):
1584added-- At this point the Rocq source defines a further
1585added-- refinement `assertion_auto''` that also rewrites with
1586added-- `leb_le`, "for inequalities". In Lean the boolean
1587added-- comparisons produced by `Bexp.eval` are already reduced
1588added-- by `simp`'s standard `decide`/`==` lemmas, so
1589added-- `assertion_auto'` handles inequalities as it stands and
1590added-- no `assertion_auto''` is needed (nor the later
1591added-- `assertion_auto'''`, whose extra `negb`/`not_false`
1592added-- rewrites `simp` also covers); occurrences of both in the
1593added-- Rocq text are rendered as `assertion_auto'`.
1594added
1595added-- Note to developers:
1596added-- HIDE: Question from 2012, Midterm 2. One-sided
1597added-- conditionals.
1598added
1599added-- ### While Loops
1600added
1601added-- The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a
1602added-- *command invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion
1603added-- whose truth is guaranteed after executing a command,
1604added-- assuming it is true before.
1605added
1606added-- That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
1607added
1608added-- {{P}} c {{P}}
1609added
1610added-- holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily
1611added-- become false in the middle of executing `c`, but by the end
1612added-- of `c` it must be restored.
1613added
1614added-- The Hoare while rule combines the idea of a command
1615added-- invariant with information about when guard `b` does or does
1616added-- not hold.
1617added
1618added-- {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1619added-- --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
1620added-- {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1621added
1622added-- Note to developers:
1623added-- HIDE: The big comment will not display nicely. But I
1624added-- guess it's folded...
1625added
1626addedtheorem hoare_while (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
1627added (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
1628added {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
1629added intro st st' heval hP
1630added /- We proceed by induction on `heval`, because, in the "keep
1631added looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
1632added of just `c`. The auxiliary statement `key` generalizes over an
1633added arbitrary command, together with an equation remembering that the
1634added command is the original loop; otherwise, that information would
1635added be lost in the induction. The cases for commands other than
1636added `while` are dismissed because their equations are contradictory. -/
1637added have key : ∀ (cmd : Com) (s s' : State), (s =[ cmd ]=> s') →
1638added cmd = (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) → P s →
1639added P s' ∧ ¬ bassertion b s' := by
1640added intro cmd s s' hev
1641added induction hev with
1642added | whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
1643added intro heq hp
1644added injection heq with e1 _
1645added subst e1
1646added exact ⟨hp, bexp_eval_false _ _ hb⟩
1647added | whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1648added intro heq hp
1649added injection heq with e1 e2
1650added subst e1 e2
1651added exact ih2 rfl (hhoare _ _ hc ⟨hp, hb⟩)
1652added | skip s0 => intro heq; simp at heq
1653added | asgn s0 a n x h => intro heq; simp at heq
1654added | seq c1 c2 s0 s0' s0'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => intro heq; simp at heq
1655added | ifTrue s0 s0' b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
1656added | ifFalse s0 s0' b0 c1 c2 hb hc ih => intro heq; simp at heq
1657added exact key _ st st' heval rfl hP
1658added
1659added-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
1660added-- This definition / discussion could be clearer.
1661added
1662added-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2023):
1663added-- `Maja says: The wording of "we will never enter the
1664added-- loop" could definitely be improved. As is, it suggests a situation
1665added-- where the loop condition itself can never be satisfied. I suspect that
1666added-- a previous draft included a discussion that explicitly placed {{ P }}
1667added-- before the while, perhaps along the lines of "a loop invariant P of
1668added-- [while b do c end] is also an invariant of [while b do c end]" (which
1669added-- is, FWIW, a (somewhat obtuse) way of stating a weaker variant of
1670added-- hoare_while, without the ~b in the postcondition). Combined with the
1671added-- fact that it is supposed to justify a somewhat surprising and
1672added-- unexpected fact — [X = 0] is not what I would intuitively consider an
1673added-- invariant of this loop — this sentence ends up being quite confusing.
1674added-- I only understood it when I came back to find this excerpt.`
1675added
1676added-- We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
1677added
1678added-- {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1679added
1680added-- is a valid Hoare triple.
1681added
1682added-- This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body
1683added-- whenever the loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`,
1684added-- this holds trivially since the precondition is false.
1685added
1686added-- For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
1687added
1688added-- while X = 2 do X := 1 end
1689added
1690added-- since the program will never enter the loop.
1691added
1692added-- _Quiz:_
1693added
1694added-- Is the assertion
1695added
1696added-- Y = 0
1697added
1698added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1699added
1700added-- while X < 100 do X := X + 1 end
1701added
1702added-- (A) Yes
1703added
1704added-- (B) No
1705added
1706added-- _Quiz:_
1707added
1708added-- Is the assertion
1709added
1710added-- X = 0
1711added
1712added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1713added
1714added-- while X < 100 do X := X + 1 end
1715added
1716added-- (A) Yes
1717added
1718added-- (B) No
1719added
1720added-- _Quiz:_
1721added
1722added-- Is the assertion
1723added
1724added-- X < Y
1725added
1726added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1727added
1728added-- while true do X := X + 1; Y := Y + 1 end
1729added
1730added-- (A) Yes
1731added
1732added-- (B) No
1733added
1734added-- _Quiz:_
1735added
1736added-- Is the assertion
1737added
1738added-- X = Y + Z
1739added
1740added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1741added
1742added-- while Y > 10 do Y := Y - 1; Z := Z + 1 end
1743added
1744added-- (A) Yes
1745added
1746added-- (B) No
1747added
1748added-- Note to developers (before next release):
1749added-- This last quiz should be turned into a discussion in the
1750added-- text, at least in the full version -- indeed, maybe all
1751added-- these should be turned into a long discussion of what it
1752added-- means to be a loop invariant -- I think that would be
1753added-- pretty helpful.
1754added
1755added-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
1756added-- What is this example doing here?? Needs some text.
1757added
1758added-- Note to developers:
1759added-- `HIDE: CJC: Maybe also a good place to talk about the structure of
1760added-- our logic - that we've set up the hoare_* lemmas and they are all
1761added-- the reasoning about Hoare triples that they should have to use (in
1762added-- both formal or informal proofs)? Probably should talk about this
1763added-- somewhere or else we'll get back lots of proofs that unfold
1764added-- ValidHoareTriple and reason at a low level everywhere.
1765added--
1766added-- BCP 21: I think we do this now?`
1767added
1768added-- _Quiz:_
1769added
1770added-- Is the assertion
1771added
1772added-- X > 0
1773added
1774added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1775added
1776added-- while X = 0 do X := X - 1 end
1777added
1778added-- (A) Yes
1779added
1780added-- (B) No
1781added
1782added-- _Quiz:_
1783added
1784added-- Is the assertion
1785added
1786added-- X < 100
1787added
1788added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1789added
1790added-- while X < 100 do X := X + 1 end
1791added
1792added-- (A) Yes
1793added
1794added-- (B) No
1795added
1796added-- _Quiz:_
1797added
1798added-- Is the assertion
1799added
1800added-- X > 10
1801added
1802added-- a loop invariant of the following?
1803added
1804added-- while X > 10 do X := X + 1 end
1805added
1806added-- (A) Yes
1807added
1808added-- (B) No
1809added
1810added-- Note to developers:
1811added-- HIDE: I (BCP) think I see a much simpler way to do the
1812added-- 'for' stuff. Instead of `for x from a to b do c` define
1813added-- `for x downfrom a do c` that steps from a down to 0.
1814added-- This will be much simpler to specify, though still an
1815added-- interesting challenge. (CJC: This still seemed hard to
1816added-- me, but I'm deleting it for now to get things looking
1817added-- right)
1818added--
1819added-- HIDE: Coming up with the precise rule for REPEAT is
1820added-- tricky, and so is proving formally that the precise rule
1821added-- passes the litmus test (at this point we only ask them
1822added-- to convince themselves informally there).
1823added
1824added-- ## Summary
1825added
1826added-- The rules of Hoare Logic are:
1827added
1828added-- --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1829added-- {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
1830added
1831added-- -------------------- (hoare_skip)
1832added-- {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
1833added
1834added-- {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
1835added-- {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
1836added-- ---------------------- (hoare_seq)
1837added-- {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
1838added
1839added-- {{P ∧ b}} c1 {{Q}}
1840added-- {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1841added-- ------------------------------------ (hoare_if)
1842added-- {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1843added
1844added-- {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1845added-- ----------------------------------- (hoare_while)
1846added-- {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
1847added
1848added-- {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1849added-- P ->> P'
1850added-- Q' ->> Q
1851added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence)
1852added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1853added
1854added-- Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules
1855added-- of Hoare logic, and prove that the definitions are sound.
1856added-- Having done so, we can go on and work *within* Hoare logic
1857added-- to prove that particular programs satisfy particular Hoare
1858added-- triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how Hoare logic is
1859added-- can be used to prove that more interesting programs satisfy
1860added-- interesting specifications of their behavior.
1861added
1862added-- Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing the
1863added-- definition of Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules
1864added-- of Hoare logic as a closed world for reasoning about
1865added-- programs.
1866added

21added/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
22addeddeclare_syntax_cat invAlt
23addedsyntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt

25added/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
26added expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
27addeddeclare_syntax_cat invAlts
28addedsyntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
29added
30added/--
31added `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,
32added then solves away contradictory generated goals.
33added `t` itself will also be generalized with a heterogeneous equality `heq`
34added if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.
35added * If `inversion +clear t` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
36added along with `t` if there are no dependencies on it.
37added * The form `inversion t with | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...` is supported,
38added similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.
39added-/
40addedsyntax (name := inversion)
41added "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (colGe invAlts)+)? : tactic
42added

45addednamespace Lean.Meta
46added
47added/--
48added This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
49added form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
50added each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
51added and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
52added It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
53added
54added This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
55added - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
56added - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
57added - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
58added
59added Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
60added-/
61addeddef forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
62added (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
63added MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
64added let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
65added unless ms.size == 1 do
66added if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
67added else throwError m!"Failed"
68added let mut mvs := ms
69added let mut bis := bs
70added let mut out : Expr := tp
71added while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
72added let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
73added unless ms.size == 1 do
74added throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
75added mvs := mvs ++ ms
76added bis := bis ++ bs
77added out := tp
78added return (mvs, bis, out)
79added
80added/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
81addeddef _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
82added let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
83added return decl.userName
84added
85added/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
86added unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
87added but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
88added This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
89added While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
90added decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
91added
92added Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
93addedpartial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
94added match eqs with
95added | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
96added | eq :: eqs =>
97added let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
98added | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
99added let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
100added let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
101added unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
102added
103added/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
104addeddef unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
105added subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
106added let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
107added let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
108added if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
109added else return some { s with
110added mvarId := mvarId,
111added subst := subst,
112added fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
113added }
114added
115added/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
116added using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
117added
118added As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context. -/
119addeddef casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
120added subgoals.mapM fun s => do
121added let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
122added let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
123added return { s with mvarId }
124added
125addedend Lean.Meta

127addednamespace Lean.Elab.Tactic
128addedopen Meta Term
129added
130added-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
131added-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
132added/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
133addedmacro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
134added
135added/--
136added `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
137added Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
138added metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
139added then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
140added original `i`.
141added
142added Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
143added-/
144addedelab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
145added let f ← elabTermForApply t
146added let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
147added | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
148added let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
149added for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
150added if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
151added try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
152added catch _ => continue
153added let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
154added (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
155added let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
156added replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
157added
158addedstructure InversionConfig where
159added clear : Bool := false
160added
161addeddeclare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
162added
163addedopen Cases in
164addeddef inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List CasesSubgoal) := withMainContext do
165added let goal ← getMainGoal
166added goal.withContext do
167added let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
168added | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
169added -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
170added if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
171added let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
172added let subgoals ← if config.clear
173added then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
174added else pure subgoals
175added return subgoals.toList
176added -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
177added else
178added let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
179added let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
180added let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
181added | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
182added let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
183added let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
184added let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
185added let subgoals ← if config.clear
186added then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
187added else pure subgoals
188added return subgoals.toList
189added
190added/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
191added solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
192added throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
193addeddef evalInvAlt (goals : List CasesSubgoal) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
194added match alt with
195added | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
196added if let some goal := goals.find? (matchTag tag.getId $ ·.ctorName.getD default) then
197added return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal.mvarId]
198added else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
199added | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
200added if !goals.isEmpty then
201added goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics ·.mvarId)
202added else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
203added | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
204addedwhere
205added matchTag tag name : Bool :=
206added tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
207added trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
208added let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
209added unless goals.isEmpty do
210added reportUnsolvedGoals goals
211added return goal
212added errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
213added let goalMsgs := goals.filterMap (.ofName <$> ·.ctorName)
214added return if goals.isEmpty
215added then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
216added else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
217added
218added@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
219addedpublic meta def evalInversion : Tactic
220added | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
221added let config ← elabInversionConfig config
222added let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
223added if let some alts := alts? then
224added let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
225added for alt in expandedAlts do
226added let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
227added goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·.mvarId)
228added unless goals.isEmpty do
229added reportUnsolvedGoals $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
230added replaceMainGoal $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
231added | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
232addedwhere expandInvAlts
233added | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
234added args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
235added | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
236added
237addedend Lean.Elab.Tactic

303addedinductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
304added | nostutter0: NoStutter []
305added | nostutter1 n : NoStutter (n::[])
306added | nostutter2 a b r (hneq : a ≠ b) (h : NoStutter (b::r)) : NoStutter (a::b::r)
307added
308addedexample : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
309added intro contra
310added inversion contra with | _ contra =>
311added inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
312added apply h

315addedinductive Vec α : Nat → Type where

323addedinductive Wec α : Nat → Type where

326added

331added inversion v with
332added | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>

337addedexample (H : Bool → Nat → False) (n : Nat) : False := by

342addedexample n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by

352added| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n

10removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
11removed-- Students will run across universes, though. When looking
12removed-- at List lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13removed--
14removed-- `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
15removed--
16removed-- Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly
17removed-- ?
18removed
19removed-- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing
20removed-- functions like `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs
21removed-- like `List.length_reverse`, which use only the list's
22removed-- structure and never inspect any particular `a : α`.
23removed
24removed-- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving
25removed-- `α` completely generic, we want to partially specify its
26removed-- behavior. In Lean, this is done through a form of "ad hoc
27removed-- polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept originated
28removed-- in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from
29removed-- other languages, such as traits in Rust.
30removed
31removed-- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
32removed
33removed-- Consider the following function, which checks whether a
34removed-- natural number occurs in a list:
35removed
36removeddef List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
37removed match xs with
38removed | [] => false
39removed | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
40removed
41removedtheorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
42removed
43removedtheorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
44removed (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
45removed
46removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
47removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
48removed#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
49removed
50removed-- What if we want this to work for lists of **any** element
51removed-- type, not just `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests
52removed-- simply replacing `Nat` with a type variable `α`, but that
53removed-- produces a puzzling error:
54removed
55removed-- Note to developers:
56removed-- @dsainati - The Verso compilation is not actually
57removed-- removing this from the generated file despite th e -keep
58removed-- flag. It is, however, stripping the message guard, so
59removed-- this results in an error. Once we figure out how we are
60removed-- handling these cases, uncomment this.
61removed--
62removed-- `/--
63removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
64removed-- BEq α
65removed--
66removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
67removed-- -/
68removed-- #guard_msgs in
69removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
70removed-- match xs with
71removed-- | [] => false
72removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
73removed--
74removed-- `/--
75removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
76removed-- BEq α
77removed--
78removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
79removed-- -/
80removed-- #guard_msgs in
81removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
82removed-- match xs with
83removed-- | [] => false
84removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
85removed--
86removed-- `/--
87removed-- error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
88removed-- BEq α
89removed--
90removed-- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
91removed-- -/
92removed-- #guard_msgs in
93removed-- def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
94removed-- match xs with
95removed-- | [] => false
96removed-- | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl`
97removed
98removed-- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==`
99removed-- should behave on a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why
100removed-- shortly; for now, here's one way to sidestep the problem:
101removed-- have the caller supply the equality test to use.
102removed
103removedsf_experiment
104removed def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
105removed match xs with
106removed | [] => false
107removed | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
108removed
109removed #eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
110removed
111removed-- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and
112removed-- remember to supply, the right equality function.
113removed
114removed-- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer
115removed-- passing the function explicitly, Lean searches for one and
116removed-- provides it on its own. We specify something we want Lean to
117removed-- search for by declaring a `class` with the needed function
118removed-- as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a
119removed-- trait in Rust. Particular *implementations* of that
120removed-- interface, different ones for different types, are called
121removed-- *instances*. Finally, we add the name of that class as a
122removed-- *typeclass constraint* on the polymorphic variable that the
123removed-- function applies to. This directs Lean to use the interface
124removed-- inside the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate
125removed-- instance at call-sites to that function. Here is what this
126removed-- looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
127removed
128removeddef List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
129removed match xs with
130removed | [] => false
131removed | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
132removed
133removedtheorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
134removed
135removedtheorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
136removed (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
137removed
138removed#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
139removed
140removed-- As Lists noted when we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes
141removed-- from the `BEq` typeclass, and it's what `List.elem_poly`
142removed-- uses internally wherever it writes `==`. This is done using
143removed-- **instance implicits**, where we place a desired typeclass
144removed-- assumption in square bracket. The `[BEq α]` constraint is
145removed-- saying that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at call
146removed-- sites for the *particular* type `α` that is used. In the
147removed-- example `[0, 1].elem_poly 0`, this type is `Nat`, and the
148removed-- automatically chosen instance corresponds to `Nat.beq`.
149removed
150removed-- Note to developers (xhalo32):
151removed-- This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`,
152removed-- which comes from `DecidableEq`, does not contain
153removed-- `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of `List.elem_nat`
154removed-- versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
155removed-- how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
156removed
157removed-- In the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, `α` was fully
158removed-- generic, with no typeclass constraint — so the `==` in its
159removed-- body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and no
160removed-- single `BEq` instance can do that. That's why Lean's search
161removed-- failed.
162removed
163removed-- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen
164removed-- so far. We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in
165removed-- below, starting with how to define a typeclass in the first
166removed-- place.
167removed
168removed-- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
169removed
170removed-- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a
171removed-- typeclass of our own, to see the mechanism — classes,
172removed-- instances, and synthesis — that made `==` resolve
173removed-- automatically above.
174removed
175removed-- Suppose we want to specify that a type has at least one
176removed-- inhabitant, i.e., that it is not empty. A `structure`
177removed-- (chapter Lists) can express this directly:
10added-- without any further information about the details of the
11added-- type `α`. Here we are able to work with a type like
12added-- `List α`, and can write functions like `List.reverse` or
13added-- `List.length` that only operate on the structure of a list
14added-- independently of its contents. Along with these we have
15added-- corresponding proofs like `List.length_reverse` that are
16added-- similarly structural in nature.
17added
18added-- This is somewhat limiting, as we cannot inspect or
19added-- non-trivially use any particular `a : α`. What we might want
20added-- in some situations rather than `α` being completely generic
21added-- is to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this happens
22added-- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called
23added-- **typeclasses**. This concept originated in the Haskell
24added-- programming language, and is analogous to features you may
25added-- be familiar with in other languages such as traits in Rust.
26added

330added-- order to write a function that uses the notation for boolean
331added-- equality over a generic type, we need a way to express that
332added-- there is some instance for `BEq α`. This is done using
333added-- **instance implicits**, where we place a desired typeclass
334added-- assumption in square brackets. Our corrected definition is
335added-- then

341added | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl

603removed-- Explanation of the infinite loop by Yipeng Liu
604removed-- (berberman): To see why, with
605removed-- `trace.Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite` enabled and specifying
606removed-- maxSteps to simp, we can track what's going on:
607removed--
608removed-- `[Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
609removed-- m a
610removed-- ==>
611removed-- m[a]
612removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
613removed-- m[a]
614removed-- ==>
615removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
616removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
617removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
618removed-- ==>
619removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
620removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
621removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
622removed-- ==>
623removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
624removed-- [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
625removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
626removed-- ==>...`
627removed--
628removed-- So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too
629removed-- board, causing this lemma repeating itself. First we
630removed-- have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is defeq to
631removed-- (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m
632removed-- to be a TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this
633removed-- lemma applies again --
634removed-- `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]`
635removed-- which is `(MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]`
636removed-- and keep going.
